body: Working in agencies, I kept seeing the same problem: designers didn't understand the medium they were designing for, devs chose to avoid learning basic visual fundamentals, and the whole team spent three times the energy for outcomes that didn't measure up. More meetings weren't going to fix it. If your designers are mad because the devs used 18px instead of 16px, there's a bigger systems problem.

I got a little obsessed with that problem. I'd seen companies that practiced pair programming, and it felt natural that design, development, and product should work that closely too. What would eventually get called the product trio made complete sense to me. I tried integrating those workflows into the teams I was on, but it's hard to change habits once everyone settles into their corners. Eventually I thought: there should be a school that teaches the whole thing together from the beginning.

So I built one. I designed the curriculum, programmed the platform, built the business and the systems behind it, and spent years working through real problems with hundreds of designers and developers. The thesis was pretty simple: the work gets better when we're one team instead of “designers” and “coders” handing things back and forth.

I kept doing product work in parallel: a green-field real estate platform where the forms, legal machinery, seller education, messaging, and the actual product all had to be figured out together; a financial education company with its experience scattered across a bunch of disconnected tools; accessibility R&D; interactive products and internal systems. The surface problem changes every time. The deeper work is figuring out what's actually going on, what matters, who needs what, and how all of those pieces should work together.

I research the problem, work through the IA and flows, design the interface, prototype in code, and work with LLMs and agents to get ideas into a form where we can test what we thought we knew. We can always flip through Mobbin and find some nice UI flourishes. The bigger gains come from getting the system right: the goals, the information, the workflows, the decisions, and the way the team works together.

I've spent about 15 years learning this product design stuff in pretty obsessive detail. I don't need to be the person doing every part. I want to understand the parts well enough to help everyone do their best work. Give me the messy problem, the people who understand different pieces of it, a whiteboard, Figma, some code — whatever we need to make the idea real enough to test, measure, and refine. My job is to make sure everybody has what they need to succeed, we're learning from each other, and we're actually getting closer to the goal.

I've spent most of my career moving back and forth between design and engineering. Sometimes I start by figuring out what something should be and then how to build it. Sometimes I get the thing working first and come back around to the interface and visual system. Depending on the year, people called that a front-end developer, creative technologist, product designer, or just the person who could figure it out.

Some years that meant building a weird interactive thing for a campaign that only needed to live for a few weeks. Other times it meant designing something that had to become a real system and survive years of new features, new people, and changing requirements. Doing both taught me when to move fast, when to slow down, how much system the thing needs, and how to leave it in a state the next person can understand and keep working on.

Eventually I got interested enough in that overlap to build a school around it. At Perpetual Education, I taught designers how the web actually works and developers how typography, hierarchy, interaction, and visual systems work. Teaching it over and over also gave me a ridiculous amount of time to test my own ideas about how design and engineering should fit together. Learning both together is actually easier. You start to understand why the other person is making the decisions they're making.

The scale of that work depends on the product and the team. Sometimes the gap is down at the HTML level: what a screen reader announces, how an interaction behaves, or getting a tiny animation right. Sometimes it's much bigger: architecture, component systems, or how something needs to work across products and platforms. I'm comfortable moving between those levels.

You can hand me a drawing on a napkin and we can start there: figure out how the thing should work, get enough of the foundation in place to try it, and then get everybody in there pushing it around. These days that might mean Figma, code, an agent, or some combination of all three. On a larger team, maybe my part is much narrower. That's fine too. I don't care whose idea wins. I care that we can actually try the ideas, find out what works, and write down what we learned.

After about 15 years of this, pull me into the weird meeting. Show me the thing that's driving everybody nuts. I'll figure out where I can be useful, get the right people involved, and help get it unstuck.

I learned to build for the web by digging through Stack Overflow threads, documentation, blog posts, and whatever else I could find. Sometimes I'd lose days, even weeks, trying to understand something, finally get it working, and realize... wait, that's it?

That happened enough times that I got really interested in why some explanations work and others don't. I probably learned as much from trying to understand and answer other people's questions as I did from asking my own. The back and forth is where you tease out what someone's actually stuck on.

Eventually that turned into mentoring, then workshops, and eventually Perpetual Education, the design and programming school I built and ran for seven years. I've now worked closely with hundreds of designers and developers at every level — interviewing them, teaching them, watching them work, helping them through problems, and seeing where the tools or the explanations get in their way.

I love it. That moment when somebody's mental model changes and the thing that seemed impossible suddenly feels obvious? That's fun. The way we learn isn't by being shown the answer. It's about setting up the situation where the learning can actually happen.

I'm always learning new things and exploring whatever's next (lately, that's been deep in AI workflows), and I do it as a working product designer and developer. So whether the job is writing docs, interviewing users, designing an example project, making a tutorial, kicking the tires on a new product, doing some weird R&D, running a workshop, or figuring out why everybody keeps getting stuck on the same feature: I'm here for it.

I don't really think of advocacy as explaining features, and it's not a one-way relationship. If I'm hearing the same question twenty times, or watching people invent the same workaround, or somebody uses the product in a way we never expected, I want to know why. I want to learn the thing with people: find the weird edges, explore the options, prototype and test, and bring everything we learn back to the people building it.
I can talk to the designer, the developer, the CEO, the person who's completely new, the experts, and the team building the product. I want all of them to understand each other a little better.
That sounds like a pretty great job to me.

Education has been this weird recurring thing in my life. I grew up in an alternative elementary program with mixed-grade classrooms, flexible learning paths, older kids teaching younger kids, and a surprising amount of learning through games. Later I went to an arts high school, designed my own major in college, then basically taught myself the web through forums, documentation, and other people on the internet.

By the time I started designing curriculum myself, I'd also spent years looking at online courses and talking to bootcamp grads, CS students, designers, and developers about what they'd learned, what they hadn't, and where they were getting stuck. What doesn't work and why, how you organize information, when you give someone an answer and when you let them struggle with it — I've spent a frankly unreasonable amount of my life thinking about this stuff.

The funny thing is, I eventually realized I'd rebuilt a lot of my elementary school at Perpetual Education. Peer teaching. People moving at different speeds. Milestones and skill trees instead of everyone marching through the same sequence. It wasn't intentional. Those were just the things that kept working.

Even my client work kept landing in education: game-based learning systems for insurance customers, a financial education platform, accessibility teaching tools, and a design-system audit for School Loop, the platform a huge share of American high schools ran on.

That's why Outsmart caught my attention. You're not just building education software. You're asking what college should look like now. I spent seven years asking a smaller version of that question, and I'd love to work on it with Product, Engineering, Academics, and people who have spent their careers thinking about parts of education I haven't.

I've spent about 15 years learning this product design stuff in pretty obsessive detail. I don't need to be the person doing every part. I want to understand the parts well enough to help everyone do their best work. Give me the messy problem, the people who understand different pieces of it, a whiteboard, Figma, some code — whatever we need to make the idea real enough to test, measure, and refine. My job is to make sure everybody has what they need to succeed, we're learning from each other, and we're actually getting closer to the goal.

I've used Vercel, Netlify, Forge, and just about every deployment option first as a freelancer, then in agencies, then as an educator. I'd guess I've onboarded into more hosting, CMSs, languages, libraries, and frameworks than most - and then I've also watched hundreds of students go through that process too. It was part of a curriculum I wrote that they'd have to take screenshots through the whole journey of whatever hosting company they choose (Heroku, Railway, Spinup). So, yes - I'm a product designer, but I'm also your target audience as a web developer or founder.

I'm a big fan of solutions that take the boilerplate and configuration out of the way and help you get things shipped. I don't want to futz around with the build config (brunch, webpack, vite, whatever) or the env variables. But I don't want to just use a black box that gives me anxiety either - so, that's where I'd see this role focusing.

Kathy Sierra's book: Badass: Making Users Awesome - is one of my favorites. I think that education as a way to level your users up in the ecosystem, create connection, and build long-term relationships is key to making them feel confident in the system / and connected to its value. That's going to involve some clear education on your agentic approach.

There are thousands of tutorials out there that get people to sign up without them really understanding what they're getting. Even at twenty dollars a month, people worry, start a project, end a project, start a project, end a project. The work is: help them understand the value, feel safe and trusting, and know their projects can scale and grow with the company. The outcome is that everybody loves working with Vercel and feels like they're getting a ridiculous amount of value. Sure, that all involves UI and visual language and design systems - but I think that underlying story and the way it's told is what will make the impact you need.

I've designed and built smaller end-to-end systems - and I've audited huge systems / so, I've worked at many different scopes. I think at Vercel, I'd have the resources to focus on this scope and knock it out of the park. I'm open to working sessions, short-term try outs and other forward thinking ways to find the best candidates without months of expensive interview theatrics.

I used LegalZoom to form my company, Perpetual Education, in 2019 (which just happens to teach web design and design systems). So this role caught my attention twice: once as a customer, and once because maintainable, CMS-driven design systems have been a core focus of my work from the start.

Reading your posting closely, the job is making the marketing surface genuinely efficient: the people working in the CMS can put content where it belongs, the right components and modules appear, and everything is styled by one underlying token system. I've spent years building exactly that: sections with their own choices, reusable modules with their own submodules, and design tokens that are relative to where you are in the page, so you maintain about fifty tokens instead of hundreds (or thousands). I've worked with a wide range of classic, headless, and unique CMSs, so Builder.io will be quick to pick up. Before applying, I read the rendered output of your marketing pages, and I see real opportunities, especially in structure and accessibility. I can help make that happen.

The part I'd push hardest: a design system succeeds as a team of teams, not as one web designer's artifact. Engineers, product designers, and the people updating content all need to understand the system, use it, and actually enjoy using it. It's not just the front-facing marketing page, the whole thing is an application itself.

On AI: I've used it daily for years, I teach it, and I've built real full-stack apps driving agents, so my outlook is mature. I've seen where it can act as a force multiplier - and where it lets everyone create a big mess. This work is what it's genuinely good at. Once we establish the system's rules, AI can audit and migrate component by component, and we can test that the results hold. Human-in-the-loop, humans learning from each other and taking that value forward with the company.

My strengths are the system itself: typography patterns, hierarchy, responsive design, and accessibility baked in from the start. I assume you have brand-focused designers I'd be working with, and part of the job as I see it is making sure their work lands coherently in the system.
I'm nearby. An hour of conversation or a working session together will tell you more than any resume, and I'd welcome either.

I've always been a champion of creators. I would force my art school friends to give me their slides and make websites for them - and our bands. Some of my favorite times were in the days of MySpace, and I've enjoyed some of that cross over in the talks from Patreon's founder. I'm interested in tech that helps build a healthy economy and that helps people flourish. Beyond this specific role, I've got some ideas and sometimes I think that Patreon is a place that could grow them.

I've also been on the creator side of it myself. For the last six years I've run Perpetual Education, a school I designed from scratch. I think designers and developers can pair and make better stuff - faster, and I think I've proven it.

I started as a developer and moved into design, so working closely with Product and Engineering is natural for me. What would eventually get called the product trio always made complete sense to me. We can always flip through Mobbin and find some nice UI flourishes. The bigger gains come from getting the system right. I'm about the goals, the information, the workflows, and the way the team works together (and making it look cool is fun too).

I'm a day-one adopter of agentic workflows and use AI in my work every day. I've seen what it can do, and also what it makes worse. What I care about is using it to help teams move faster without losing the shared understanding that good product decisions depend on.
I'm open to working sessions, short-term try outs and other forward thinking ways to find the best candidates without months of expensive interview theatrics.
